Did you know? Aquatic adaptations
River otters have a “third eyelid” called a nictitating membrane that allows them to see while they’re underwater. Their ears and nostrils also close to keep water out.

The river otter isn’t the only species that appears to be making a comeback on the Bronx River. In 2007, a beaver returned to the river for the first time in more than 200 years. The creature, nicknamed José after then-U.S. Representative José E. Serrano of the Bronx, was joined a few years later by another dubbed Justin Beaver. But the pair vanished around 2018.

Beavers weren’t seen again on the river until May 2025, when one of Hawkins’ camera traps captured one. And this summer, one of his cameras photographed an American mink—another freshwater ecosystem indicator species.

“What we were able to do and what the community was able to do is to give a little bit of respite to nature,” John Calvelli, executive vice president of public affairs for WCS, tells Gothamist. “And guess what? Nature is incredibly resilient. If we give it some time, it will come back.”

| Daily Correspondent

September 23, 2026 2:06 p.m.

He decided to run the image by experts at the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation and WCS. They agreed—his camera had indeed captured a North American river otter, the first sighting of the species along the Bronx River since the early 1900s.
